event: The 2nd Marine Division storms Betio, Tarawa Atoll, where a neap tide its New Zealand adviser had warned of leaves the boats stranded on the reef and the Marines wading hundreds of yards under fire; 76 hours later the island falls
place: Betio, Tarawa Atoll, Gilbert Islands (now Kiribati)
why: A warning about the tide that came true, an assault that nearly failed on the reef, named men whose choices turned it (Holland, Shoup, Hawkins, Bonnyman, Bordelon), a cost in 76 hours that shocked the country, and a long coda in which Bonnyman's lost grave was found in 2015; far more than cards No. 74, 75 and 79 could hold.
alternates: The battleship night of the Naval Battle of Guadalcanal, 14 to 15 November 1942: USS Washington, under Rear Adm. Willis Lee, wrecks the battleship Kirishima by radar gunfire while South Dakota is battered; the account covered it in cards No. 57 and 58, so the article would need the night action in full.

Operation Uranus, 19 November 1942: the Soviet pincers close around the German Sixth Army at Stalingrad in four days; covered by cards No. 71 to 73, and short of named individual stories in strong English language sources.

facts.text: On the morning of 20 November 1943 the 2nd Marine Division, under Maj. Gen. Julian C. Smith, assaulted Betio, the fortified main island of Tarawa Atoll in the Gilberts, in Operation Galvanic.

Whatever the approach, every boat had to cross a coral reef. The critical depth over it was four feet, enough to float a loaded Higgins boat (LCVP); with less, the troops would have to wade several hundred yards under fire.
For tide information the division turned to men who had lived and sailed there, among them Maj. Frank Holland, a New Zealand reserve officer who had lived on Bairiki, next to Betio, for 15 years.
The tide tables led General Smith to expect 5 feet of water over the reef at high neap tide, but he was also warned that the tides were not dependable and that there were frequent dodging tides.

Holland flatly predicted there would not be three feet of water on the reef. Col. David M. Shoup took the warning seriously and made sure the troops knew there was a 50 to 50 chance of having to wade ashore.

At the Pearl Harbor planning conference, Admiral Nimitz limited the preliminary bombardment to about three hours on the morning of D Day for the sake of surprise, and ruled out seizing neighboring Bairiki first and any decoy landing. Then Maj. Gen. Holland Smith announced the 6th Marines would be held back as corps reserve.
Left with only a 2 to 1 superiority in troops, below the doctrinal minimum, a shaken Julian Smith insisted that Holland Smith absolve him of responsibility for the consequences. This was done.

Only amphibian tractors (amtracs, LVTs) could be counted on to climb the reef, so they carried the first three waves; later waves had to come in boats. The division had about 100 tractors, 75 of them thought fit, and 50 new LVT 2s were rushed to Samoa to meet it at Tarawa.

Just before H Hour, 1st Lt. William Deane Hawkins and his Scout Sniper Platoon, with a squad of engineers under Lt. A. G. Leslie, charged up the long pier at the reef's edge and cleared its machine gun nests with explosives and flamethrowers, about 15 minutes before any troops reached the beach. Leslie's flamethrower set the pier on fire.
Naval gunfire was almost entirely lifted for the final 25 minutes of the run in, giving the defenders time to shift troops from the south and west beaches to the north shore.

The first amtracs touched down at 9:10 a.m. on Red Beach One. Only 8 of the 87 tractors in the first three waves were lost going in, and within about 10 minutes they had landed more than 1,500 Marines.
Major Holland's prediction proved right: no landing craft crossed the reef all day on D Day. After about 10 a.m. most troops had to wade from the reef, 500 to 1,000 yards, under well aimed fire.
Maj. Drewes, the amtrac battalion commander who had worked with Shoup to make the tractor assault possible, took over a machine gun from a fallen gunner and was killed instantly.
At 9:59 a.m. Maj. Schoettel, commanding the landing team off Red Beach One, radioed Shoup: "Receiving heavy fire all along beach. Unable to land all. Issue in doubt."
Time correspondent Robert Sherrod waded in with the fourth wave on Red Beach Two and later wrote that he had seven hundred yards to walk slowly into machine gun fire.
Shoup set up his command post on the blind side of a Japanese bunker that was still occupied. At least two dozen messengers were shot carrying dispatches to and from him.
At 1:31 p.m. on D Day General Smith radioed Holland Smith "situation in doubt" and asked for the 6th Marines to be released to him.

SSgt. William Bordelon, a combat engineer whose amtrac was hit on the way in, led the survivors ashore, knocked out positions with demolition charges, went back into the water to save a wounded Marine, and was killed charging another strongpoint. He was the first of four Marines awarded the Medal of Honor for Tarawa.
On the morning of 21 November, Maj. Lawrence Hays' battalion, after about 18 hours in their boats, again found too little water over the reef and waded 500 yards into a crossfire, with heavy losses.

Hawkins, wounded by a mortar shell on D Day, refused treatment. At dawn on 21 November he crawled up to a pillbox, fired through its gun ports and threw grenades inside, was shot in the chest, kept going and took out three more pillboxes, then was mortally wounded by a shell.
Hawkins, of El Paso, Texas, was awarded the Medal of Honor after his death; it was presented on 30 August 1944. The Betio airfield was named Hawkins Field in his honor.
At 4 p.m. on 21 November Shoup sent the situation report that ended with the words that made him famous: casualties many, percentage dead unknown, combat efficiency, we are winning.

On 22 November a huge Japanese bombproof shelter near Red Beach Three held up the 8th Marines. 1st Lt. Alexander Bonnyman, Jr., led a squad of engineers up its sand covered slope, met a counterattack with his flamethrower, then charged with a carbine and was shot dead. Hundreds of Japanese then broke out of the shelter and were cut down.

Bonnyman, 33, had a war related mining business in New Mexico that exempted him from service, but enlisted as a private. His Medal of Honor was presented on 22 January 1947 and accepted by his 12 year old daughter, Frances.

Early on 22 November Rear Admiral Keiji Shibasaki sent a last message to Tokyo: his weapons were destroyed and everyone was attempting a final charge. He died in the fighting, and the date is disputed.
Organized resistance on Betio ended at 1:05 p.m. on 23 November, about 76 hours after the first amtrac, "My Deloris", reached the seawall.
Of an estimated 4,836 defenders, 4,690 were killed. Only 146 prisoners were taken: 17 wounded Japanese and 129 Korean laborers.

The 1993 Marine history gives the 2nd Marine Division's losses as 997 Marines and 30 Navy corpsmen and medical personnel killed, 88 missing and presumed dead, and 2,233 Marines and 59 sailors wounded, 3,407 in all. The 1947 Marine casualty table gives a total of 3,301.
The Guadalcanal campaign had cost the Marines a comparable number of casualties over six months; Tarawa's came in 76 hours.
The amtracs paid heavily: only 35 of the 125 used at Betio were left, and the 2nd Amphibian Tractor Battalion lost more than half its men.

Walking Red Beach One after the fighting, Chaplain W. Wyeth Willard counted the bodies of 76 Marines lying half in and half out of the water. Nearly 100 Marines were missing, many swept out to sea by the tides.
At the flag raising on Betio, Major Holland, the man who had foreseen the tide, produced the Union Jack that went up beside the American flag on two surviving palm trees.
Holland Smith toured Betio on 24 November with tears in his eyes. Beside a dead Marine at the seawall, near a beach marker flag, he asked, "How can men like that ever be defeated?"
Before dawn that same day, 24 November, the Japanese submarine I-175 torpedoed the escort carrier Liscome Bay off Makin; she sank quickly with 644 men.

At home the losses caused an uproar. Navy Secretary Frank Knox blamed a sudden shift in the wind, MacArthur called frontal attacks like Tarawa a tragic and unnecessary massacre, and Commandant Alexander Vandegrift told Congress that Tarawa was an assault from beginning to end.

Nimitz held that the capture of Tarawa knocked down the front door to the Japanese defenses in the Central Pacific. The Marshalls were invaded only 10 weeks later, and the lessons, above all the need for many more and better armored amtracs, shaped every Central Pacific landing that followed.
Marine combat cameraman SSgt. Norman Hatch filmed the fighting, and the eyewitness documentary made from his film won an Academy Award in 1944.
Bonnyman's grave on Betio was lost. In 2015 the group History Flight found the battlefield cemetery; his remains were identified that year and buried in Knoxville, Tennessee, on 27 September 2015.

quotes.text: there won't be three feet of water on the reef!
quotes.by: Maj. Frank Holland, New Zealand reserve officer and Tarawa tide adviser

quotes.text: I'm an old railbird shooter up on the marshes of the Chesapeake Bay. You push over the marshes at high tide, and when you have a neap tide, you can't get over the marshes.
surely, no mortal men could live through such destroying power
quotes.when: Morning of 20 November 1943, watching the bombardment

quotes.text: Receiving heavy fire all along beach. Unable to land all. Issue in doubt.
quotes.by: Maj. Schoettel, radio message to Col. Shoup

quotes.text: It was painfully slow, wading in such deep water. And we had seven hundred yards to walk slowly into that machine gun fire, looming into larger targets as we rose onto higher ground. I was scared, as I had never been scared before.
We're in a tight spot. We've got to have more men.
quotes.by: Col. David M. Shoup, to Robert Sherrod at his command post

quotes.text: What are they saving us for, the Junior Prom?
quotes.by: Chaplain W. Wyeth Willard, to Colonel Hall's boat

quotes.text: It's not often that you can credit a first lieutenant with winning a battle, but Hawkins came as near to it as any man could.
Casualties: many. Percentage dead: unknown. Combat efficiency: We are winning.
quotes.by: Col. David M. Shoup, situation report to Maj. Gen. Julian Smith
quotes.note: Punctuation as printed by Alexander (1993). Card No. 79 used another printed version: "Casualties many; percentage dead not known; combat efficiency: We are winning." Use one version consistently and do not mix them.

quotes.text: Our weapons have been destroyed and from now on everyone is attempting a final charge.... May Japan exist for 10,000 years!
quotes.by: Rear Admiral Keiji Shibasaki, last message to Tokyo (from Japanese archives)

quotes.text: Along the shore I counted the bodies of 76 Marines staring up at me, half in, half out of the water.
quotes.note: Alexander prints it as: "Along the shore," he wrote, "I counted the bodies of 76 Marines staring up at me, half in, half out of the water."

quotes.text: How can men like that ever be defeated?
quotes.by: Maj. Gen. Holland M. Smith, on Betio

quotes.text: Tarawa was an assault from beginning to end.
quotes.by: Gen. Alexander A. Vandegrift, Commandant of the Marine Corps, to Congress
quotes.when: In the weeks after the battle

quotes.text: The capture of Tarawa knocked down the front door to the Japanese defenses in the Central Pacific.
quotes.note: Alexander prints: "The capture of Tarawa," he stated, "knocked down the front door to the Japanese defenses in the Central Pacific."

quotes.text: He gallantly gave his life for his country.
quotes.by: Medal of Honor citation of 1st Lt. Alexander Bonnyman, Jr.
